readings.title: Comparing rainfall in two gardens
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Neighbours placed rain gauges in two gardens. One gauge reported much more rain after every shower, although the houses stood close together. The main obstacle was gauges installed in different positions. One sat beneath a roof edge where runoff could fall into it. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a supervised relocation and comparison. The group placed instruments in open positions and recorded readings after the same showers. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated placement explained the large difference. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a common installation guide for volunteers. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: measurement quality begins before recording numbers. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in comparing rainfall in two gardens, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A forecast for a school trip
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A teacher checked a weather forecast before a school trip. The chance of rain was low, but the planned route had little shelter. The main obstacle was a probability treated as a guarantee. The initial plan included no response if a brief shower occurred. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a review of forecast uncertainty and route options. Staff compared safe alternatives and consulted the school trip guidance. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated a simple backup plan protected the outing. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a sheltered stop and a clear decision time. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: uncertain forecasts still support careful planning. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in a forecast for a school trip, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A heat map for town streets
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Students mapped air temperature in a town. Their first results made a tree-lined street look hotter than a nearby paved square. The main obstacle was readings taken at different hours. The shaded street was measured late in the afternoon while the square was visited early. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used repeat measurements on a shared timetable. Students used the same height and recorded cloud and shade conditions. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated the revised map showed a different pattern. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a published method beside the temperature map. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: a fair comparison needs consistent timing. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a heat map for town streets, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Reading a storm alert colour
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A weather office used colours to indicate storm risk. Some residents understood the colour but not what action their neighbourhood required. The main obstacle was a warning scale without local examples. The message described wind strength but did not mention loose outdoor objects or travel changes. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used questions collected after a practice alert. Staff asked residents what they planned to do and compared answers with official guidance. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated action examples improved the message. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a short local checklist linked to each alert. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: science communication connects evidence to decisions. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in reading a storm alert colour, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the community weather learning programme, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about weather observation and scientific judgement, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.

translation.referenceAnswer: 社区调整一项服务时，简短解释可能和改动本身同样重要。人们想知道发现了什么问题、如何收集信息，以及为何选择某个方案。在一个有关天气观测与科学判断的项目中，工作人员观察实际使用，而不只依靠图纸或最初的承诺。证据揭示了起初并不明显的障碍。组织者作出有限调整，并告知居民何时重新评估。他们也说明试行的局限，因为少量使用经历不能代表未来所有情况。诚实的说明让这项决定更容易被讨论和改进。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the weather observation team suggesting a practical change to the community weather learning programme. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community weather learning programme. People have noticed gauges installed in different positions, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
